items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the not-for-profit corporation law, in relation to powers and dissolution of land banks
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S7589

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the not-for-profit corporation law, in relation to
powers and dissolution of land banks

 PURPOSE :

To authorize the land banks to lend money and make grants as well as
to allow land banks to organize subsidiaries and hold title to
property in the name of the subsidiaries.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section one adds two sections to § 1607 of the Not-For-Profit
Corporation Law that would authorize the land banks to lend money and
make grants and to organize subsidiaries.

Section two amends § 1609 of the Not-For-Profit Corporation Law to
allow land banks to hold title to property in the name of the lawfully
organized subsidiaries.

Section three provides the immediate effective date.

 EXISTING LAW :

Article 16 of the Not-For-Profit Corporation Law provides for the
powers of land banks.

 JUSTIFICATION :

The Authority Budget Office has taken the position that local public
authorities, which include land banks, do not have the power to lend
money or make grants unless expressly authorized to do so by enabling
legislation, even when such actions are in furtherance of an
enumerated purpose. An amendment is proposed to the Land Bank Act
granting land banks the power to make grants and loans for the
following reasons:

*The ability of land banks to offer grants and loans for
mission-related purposes will both enhance and accelerate the return
of tax delinquent, vacant and abandoned property to productive tax
paying use.
*Grants or loans made to the purchasers of land bank property will
provide an additional incentive to attract certain desired buyers
(e.g. owner-occupants) who might not otherwise be interested in the
subject property and grants and loans will also provide a method to
enhance development outcomes consistent with the land bank's mission
and purpose (e.g. a higher quality exterior renovation than the market
might otherwise bear in order to support neighborhood revitalization).
*The ability of land banks to offer grants and loans for exterior
improvements to property owners in the same neighborhood or area of
land bank owned properties will improve market-confidence in the
neighborhood or area and support revitalization.
*In recent years, municipalities have deliberately outsourced this
type of community revitalization work to more nimble not-for-profit
entities and no longer wish to be in the business of making grants and
loans directly. Land banks' financial assets include revenue from
sources other than the municipalities that created them, including
revenue from the sale or leasing of its properties, and, as such, the
funds used for grants and loans would not necessarily come from
appropriated funds of a municipality.
*Grants and loans made by a land bank would have to be approved by the
land bank's board of directors who have a fiduciary duty to make
prudent use of land banks' limited financial resources.
*Grants and loans made directly by a land bank (rather than by a
municipality) could be better coordinated with other land bank
projects for maximum impact and would allow for grants and loans to be
made in conjunction with the sale or leasing of land bank property.

The Authority Budget Office has taken the position that local public
authorities, which include land banks, do not have the power to
organize subsidiaries unless expressly authorized to do so by enabling
legislation, even when such actions are in furtherance of an
enumerated purpose. An amendment is proposed to the Land Bank Act
granting land banks the power to organize subsidiaries under limited
circumstances and hold title to real property in the name of lawfully
organized subsidiaries as follows:
*The primary reason for which a subsidiary may be organized must be to
limit the potential liability impact of the subsidiary's project on
the land bank or because state or federal law requires that the
project of a subsidiary be undertaken through a specific corporate or
business structure. These are the same reasons state authorities are
currently permitted to form subsidiaries.
*Land banks often acquire properties for the purpose of stabilizing
and marketing them for sale. Environmental studies and testing, which
requires site-control, might be conducted during the period that the
land bank holds title. With test results in hand, the property can be
more effectively marketed to buyers who will know the extent of
remediation the priority requires. However, without the ability to
hold potentially contaminated sites in a separate business entity,
land banks are less inclined to take title to these risky properties.
If the property could be held in a separate business entity, liability
associated with such properties would be segregated from the remainder
of the land bank's assets. Use of a subsidiary would be available for
other high risk properties as well (e.g. a condemned or structurally
compromised building). A land bank's board of directors would have to
utilize their discretion when deciding if the risk associated with the
property warrants the cost of forming a subsidiary.
*Land banks have found that a single-asset business entity must be
formed in order to borrow against certain property for renovation
expenses. Lenders require this so that liabilities associated with the
rest of the land bank's inventory do not affect the property serving
as collateral for their loan.
*To ensure that subsidiaries will not result in any loss of
transparency, land banks would have to include properties held by
subsidiaries in their property inventories required by the Land Bank
Act and subject to FOIL, and in all reports made annually to the
Authorizes Budget Office. The amendment further specifies that the
name of the subsidiary must be reasonably related to the name of the
land bank of which it is a subsidiary for ease of public
identification.
*The amendment states that lawfully formed subsidiaries and properties
held by such subsidiary shall be exempt from all taxation, just as
land banks are exempt.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

To be determined

 LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

To be determined

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately
